description: Connector-layer authorization vectors for Solana user decryption: the host policy applied to a request against a recorded observation of host state.

deployment.chain_id_derivation: stand-in: the real derivation from the genesis hash is an open protocol item, and this set is regenerated once it is settled

vectors.name: direct-current
vectors.comment: The reference request: the signer names their own live handle, is a current member of its lineage, and the lineage's domain is in the signed scope.

vectors.name: delegated-current
vectors.comment: A handle owned by a delegator, used by the signer under a live delegation for the lineage's app account. The authorized subject is the delegator.

vectors.name: historical-after-supersession
vectors.comment: The handle has been superseded, and the leaf sealed for the signer at that moment proves the access. No new wallet signature is involved: proofs live outside the permit.

vectors.name: historical-proof-predating-a-non-merging-append
vectors.comment: The proof was built against an earlier leaf count and the append that followed left its peak alone, so it still verifies. Verification comes first and age alone is not a failure: rejecting this would fail valid proofs after every write.

vectors.name: permissive-scope-foreign-domain
vectors.comment: An empty signed domain list is permissive: the domain rule is skipped entirely, so a lineage of any domain is in scope. Membership still has to hold.

vectors.name: duplicate-handle
vectors.comment: Naming the same handle twice is legal: each occurrence counts toward the budget, is authorized independently, and is bound at its own position by the response.

vectors.name: mixed-direct-and-two-delegators
vectors.comment: One request freely mixes a direct entry with entries from two different delegators. There is no per-request mode and no separate delegated route.

vectors.name: many-handles-in-one-request
vectors.comment: One request naming many handles of many lineages. No layer of the Connector caps the count: the system-wide decryption budget is summed and enforced by the Gateway entry point on chain, so a request that exists has already passed it.

vectors.name: absent-invalidation-record
vectors.comment: A user who has never revoked anything has no invalidation record, and its absence reads as a watermark of zero rather than as a missing initialisation step.

vectors.name: future-start-permit-outliving-a-revocation
vectors.comment: The permit's window opens after a revocation that was performed before it opened, so the revocation does not reach it and the request is authorized. This is a recorded weakness of the watermark design, accepted for parity with the EVM path and filed as a follow-up for both — not a property this set endorses.

vectors.name: wrong-host-program
vectors.comment: A permit signed for another host program authorizes nothing here, even on the right cluster.
vectors.mutation: the permit's verifying program id is replaced with another program

vectors.name: wrong-host-chain-id
vectors.comment: A permit signed for another cluster authorizes nothing here, even under the same program id — which is why the cluster is signed at all.
vectors.mutation: the permit's chain id, and the chain id embedded in its handle, name another cluster

vectors.name: mixed-embedded-chain-ids
vectors.comment: Handles of one request must embed one chain id. A mixed batch is refused rather than resolved by taking the first handle as the truth.
vectors.mutation: a second entry is appended whose handle embeds another cluster

vectors.name: handle-of-another-cluster
vectors.comment: Handles agreeing among themselves is not enough: every embedded chain id must equal the signed one, or the request is about another cluster's ciphertexts.
vectors.mutation: the entry's handle embeds another cluster while the permit still names this one

vectors.name: expired-permit
vectors.comment: The validity window has closed. No later observation makes a permit younger.
vectors.mutation: the request is authorized after the permit's window ends

vectors.name: not-yet-valid-permit
vectors.comment: The window has not opened. Transient, because this is the one rejection that the passage of time repairs on its own.
vectors.mutation: the request is authorized before the permit's window starts

vectors.name: invalidated-permit
vectors.comment: The permit started before its signer's last revocation, so it is dead permanently. This is the mechanism behind revoking every outstanding signature with one transaction.
vectors.mutation: the signer's invalidation record holds a watermark above the permit's start

vectors.name: invalidation-record-of-another-user
vectors.comment: The invalidation record's contents are checked against the address it was read from: a record naming another user is refused rather than read as that user's watermark, and refused rather than read as zero.
vectors.mutation: the signer's invalidation address holds a record naming a different user

vectors.name: destroyed-kms-epoch
vectors.comment: Governance destroyed the epoch the permit signed. Transient, and deliberately so: the Connector learns about the pair from a single boolean that is true only when the epoch is active and belongs to the signed context, so a destroyed epoch is indistinguishable from one that is not active yet. The request is retried within the attempt budget and never succeeds — inherited behaviour of the pair validation the EVM path shares, not a decision of the Solana path, and fail-closed either way.
vectors.mutation: the KMS management state reports the signed epoch as destroyed

vectors.name: not-yet-active-kms-epoch
vectors.comment: The epoch exists but is not active yet. The reference case of the transient outcome, and the reason the two records around it share both its rule and its class: all three arrive as the same boolean.
vectors.mutation: the KMS management state reports the signed epoch as not active yet

vectors.name: kms-epoch-of-another-context
vectors.comment: The signed epoch belongs to a different context, so the pair will never be servable — and it is transient for the same reason as the destroyed epoch: the view returns one boolean, and no view exposes the epoch's context on its own.
vectors.mutation: the KMS management state reports the signed epoch as belonging to another context

vectors.name: empty-handle-list
vectors.comment: A request naming no handles has nothing to authorize and nothing for a response to bind.
vectors.mutation: the handle list is emptied

vectors.name: access-proof-with-trailing-bytes
vectors.comment: A proof followed by extra bytes is refused — unlike an account followed by extra bytes, which is legal. Two byte strings for one proof would leave two implementations disagreeing about whether they hold the same request.
vectors.mutation: two bytes are appended to the entry's access proof

vectors.name: access-proof-with-too-many-siblings
vectors.comment: The sibling count is bounded by what the tree can produce, so an untrusted request cannot make the decoder allocate an arbitrary list.
vectors.mutation: the entry's access proof carries one sibling more than the tree's height ceiling

vectors.name: malformed-access-proof
vectors.comment: Bytes that are not a proof at all are refused as a form error, before any state is read.
vectors.mutation: the entry's access proof is replaced with three arbitrary bytes

vectors.name: missing-lineage
vectors.comment: The lineage account does not exist at this observation. Transient by nature: the account may simply not have reached the observed commitment yet.
vectors.mutation: the lineage account is removed from the observation

vectors.name: lineage-owned-by-another-program
vectors.comment: Program ownership is the sole trust anchor: an account with impeccable contents under another program's ownership proves nothing.
vectors.mutation: the lineage account's owner is replaced with another program

vectors.name: delegation-record-as-lineage
vectors.comment: A host-owned account of another type is caught by the discriminator rather than by what its bytes happen to mean when read as a lineage.
vectors.mutation: the lineage address holds a delegation record instead

vectors.name: lineage-with-a-truncated-body
vectors.comment: A body cut short is not the same thing as a body followed by extra bytes: the first cannot be read, the second is an account with room to spare.
vectors.mutation: eight bytes are removed from the end of the lineage account

vectors.name: lineage-deriving-another-value-key
vectors.comment: The account's own fields must reproduce the identity that was claimed. This is the backstop that makes a substituted lineage a rejection rather than a redirection.
vectors.mutation: the lineage address holds a lineage of another app account

vectors.name: handle-of-an-unsigned-domain
vectors.comment: With a non-empty signed scope, every entry's lineage domain must be in it. The domain tested is the lineage's — a request has no field for it.
vectors.mutation: the entry names a lineage whose domain is outside the signed scope

vectors.name: superseded-current-handle
vectors.comment: A current-mode entry whose handle has been superseded fails, and is not quietly answered with whatever is current instead. The same handle remains reachable as historical access.
vectors.mutation: the lineage's current handle moves on before the observation

vectors.name: subject-outside-the-current-members
vectors.comment: Current access requires membership of the lineage's current subject set, and the set is the account's rather than the request's.
vectors.mutation: the lineage's subject set names somebody else

vectors.name: leaf-index-beyond-the-leaf-count
vectors.comment: A position the lineage does not have is refused before any hashing: there is nothing for the proof to be a proof of. From the outside this is an inclusion failure like any other, and it is classified like one — by the leaf count the request claims. Here the claim is at or above the observed count, which is what a proof service running ahead of this observation looks like, so the answer is to retry rather than to rebuild.
vectors.mutation: the proof names a leaf index equal to the observed leaf count

vectors.name: leaf-commitment-for-another-lineage
vectors.comment: A leaf sealed for another lineage account authorizes nothing here.
vectors.mutation: the sealed leaf commits to another lineage account

vectors.name: leaf-commitment-for-another-subject
vectors.comment: A leaf sealed for another subject authorizes only that subject.
vectors.mutation: the sealed leaf commits to another subject

vectors.name: leaf-commitment-for-another-handle
vectors.comment: A leaf sealed for another handle authorizes only that handle.
vectors.mutation: the sealed leaf commits to another handle

vectors.name: leaf-commitment-at-another-position
vectors.comment: A leaf whose committed position is not the position it occupies authorizes nothing.
vectors.mutation: the sealed leaf commits to leaf index one while occupying index zero

vectors.name: public-decrypt-leaf-as-historical-access
vectors.comment: Public decryptability is a separate flow with its own leaf domain. Its leaf says nothing about any subject and must not double as evidence that one held the handle.
vectors.mutation: the proof is of a public-decrypt leaf rather than a historical-access leaf

vectors.name: proof-predating-a-merging-append
vectors.comment: The append merged the proof's peak, so the sibling path it carries no longer exists. The claimed count is below the observed one, which is what tells the client to rebuild rather than to retry.
vectors.mutation: an append that merges the proof's peak happens before the observation

vectors.name: proof-ahead-of-the-observation
vectors.comment: The proof service observed more state than this observation did. The claimed count is not below the observed one, so the same request is worth repeating from a later observation — and will succeed once the view catches up.
vectors.mutation: the observation holds an earlier state than the one the proof was built against

vectors.name: missing-delegation
vectors.comment: No delegation record at the canonical address for the tuple, so the delegated entry has nothing standing behind it.
vectors.mutation: the delegation record is removed from the observation

vectors.name: revoked-delegation
vectors.comment: The delegator revoked it. Subsequent requests stop immediately, while the signer's own permit remains valid — two independent levers, one per party.
vectors.mutation: the delegation record is marked revoked

vectors.name: expired-delegation
vectors.comment: Expiry is measured against the observed slot, not against a local clock.
vectors.mutation: the delegation's expiration slot falls below the observed slot

vectors.name: delegation-newer-than-the-observation
vectors.comment: A record written after the observation is not part of the state this authorization saw. Accepting it would mean authorizing from two points in time at once.
vectors.mutation: the delegation's last update slot is above the observed slot

vectors.name: delegation-record-of-another-tuple
vectors.comment: A record sitting at the canonical address while naming a different tuple is refused: the address alone is not taken as proof of what the record says.
vectors.mutation: the delegation address holds a record naming another delegator

vectors.name: delegation-record-owned-by-another-program
vectors.comment: Only the host program grants delegations; an account under another program's ownership is not one.
vectors.mutation: the delegation record's owner is replaced with another program

vectors.name: lineage-record-as-delegation
vectors.comment: A host-owned account of another type at the delegation address is caught by its discriminator, the mirror of the same substitution against a lineage.
vectors.mutation: the delegation address holds a lineage account instead
